messages.subject: Question about facets
messages.body_plain:
I'm new to ggplot2, and I'm looking at the description of facets in the
2012 edition of R Graphics Cookbook, by Winston Chang.  From what I find
there, I'm unclear whether facets can do what I want.  Specifically, I
have a data frame with five variables, Date, y1, y2, y3, and y4.  The
y's all have different scales---they're different types of variables,
but they were all measured on the same dates.  I'd like to plot each of
the y's against Date, with the four graphs arranged one above the other.
  Is that possible with facets, as it is with lattice graphs?
David
messages.body_snippet:

messages.subject: RE: Question about facets
messages.body_plain:
You can reshape the data frame to long format   using melt and plot the 4 graphs using facets. Package reshape2 is required for the melt function. See: http://www.cookbook-r.com/Manipulating_data/Converting_data_between_wide_and_long_format/.

A reproducible example helps.

have a data frame with five variables, Date, y1, y2, y3, and y4.  The
y's all have different scales---they're different types of variables,

messages.subject: Re: Question about facets
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Vivek's reply looks pretty good to me, but since you are new to this
game, I'll explain a bit how melt() works and why it's useful in this
situation for ggplot2.

The reshape2 package is designed to manipulate data from wide to long
form (melt()) or long to wide form (acast() or dcast()). In your case,
the right call is to reshape your data frame from wide to long. The
melt() function behaves somewhat like the stack() function in base R;
when the non-id (or 'measure') variables are stacked, two variables
are created: a factor named variable, which takes the original
variable names in long form and converts them to factor levels, and a
corresponding numeric variable named value. The 'constant' variable in
your original data frame is date, so it becomes the id variable. In
the melted data frame, it is recycled as many times as the number of
stacked variables. The resulting melted data frame has three
variables: date, variable and value.

The melted data frame is passed to ggplot(). The reason why this
approach works is because the faceting variable is normally a factor.
Also notice that the code is set up to plot value vs. date by
variable; the data structure returned by melt() made this possible.
The remaining options to facet_wrap() allow for vertical stacking of
the plots (ncol = 1) and free y-scales (scales = "free_y").

You can also plot dates on the horizontal axis in ggplot2; it is smart
enough to deduce if the x-variable is of class Date and plot a
set of default labels. I don't know what the time origin is of your
dates - I guessed it was Excel's default of 1 Jan 1900 based on a
little trial and error - let's pretend it is. Using Vivek's notation,

dfmelt$Date <- as.Date(dfmelt$date, origin = "1900-01-01")
ggplot(dfmelt, aes(x = Date, y = value)) +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(~ variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y")

If the dates are wrong, modify the origin. If you want to change the
date scale, use the scale_x_date() function to change the breaks. To
change the labels, use the date_format() function from the scales
package. There are a few examples here; see section 7.1:
http://cloud.github.com/downloads/hadley/ggplot2/guide-col.pdf

You can take your set of original ggplots, assign them to distinct
objects and use the grid.arrange() function in the gridExtra package
to accomplish the same task, but the differences in the magnitudes of
the y-axis labels will cause the left-side plot boundaries to be
misaligned. There are documented ways to fix the problem using the
gtable package, but the ggplot2 solution in this case is simpler and a
bit cleaner visually. Since you are new to ggplot2, simpler is better.

Dennis

messages.subject: Rotating individual text with geom text dataframe
messages.subject_clean: Rotating individual text with geom text dataframe
messages.body_plain:
Assume the following example has n labels that need to be place inside of n boxes. Angle is a set aesthetic that can't draw its value from a data frame variable. Is there a simple way of telling geom_text to rotate specific labels? Obviously breaking it into 2 geom_text calls and 2 data sets would work... but is there something more elegant?

ex.dat<-data.frame(x1=c(200,100),
                    x2=c(300,200),
                    y1=c(0,0),
                    y2=c(0.01,0.02),
                     a=c(0,90),
                    r=c("label","rotated\nlabel"))

p<-ggplot() +
  geom_density(data=mtcars, aes(x=disp, group=cyl, fill=cyl), alpha=0.6, adjust=0.75)+
  geom_rect(data=ex.dat, aes(xmin=x1, xmax=x2, ymin=y1,ymax=y2), alpha=0, color="black" )+
  geom_text(data=ex.dat, aes(x=x1+(x2-x1)/2, y=y1+(y2-y1)/2, label=r), size=5, angle=a) #this doesn't work, but it works if you remove the "angle = a"
x11()
p

Thanks,
Thomas

Hi:

I think this problem is a bit simpler than you're making it...

On Tue, Mar 4, 2014 at 10:19 AM, Loren V <lm.vela...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I was wondering if I could perhaps do some kind of loop that will loop
> through 100 different locations and give me graphs of how many people visit
> a location and for that location give me the number of males and females
> that visit that location.
>
> Suppose that:
> -this data is stored in a csv files and i read it into R in a variable
> called data
> - data$gender has male and female data so that when i do table(data$gender)
> i get the total overall number of females and males that visit each location
> - data$location has these individual locations

>
> gender_location <- by(data$gender,data$location,summary)

The problem with by() is that it returns a list, and you can't input a
list directly into ggplot2 - it has to be converted to a data frame
first.

The plyr package, also authored by Hadley Wickham, is a very good one
for basic data summarization. In this case, you could use the count()
function in that package to get the counts by location and gender
(which would return a data frame), but I would take it a bit further.
Rather than trying to plot bars and pies at each location, plot points
of the percentage of one gender instead. If the total number of
visitors is meaningful, then you could use something like color to
indicate percentage and point size to visualize the number of
visitors. They can be done together in ggplot2.

Inferring from your message, it appears that something like

library(plyr)
loccts <- count(data, c("location", "gender"))

would produce the frequencies and then

loccts <- ddply(loccts, .(location), mutate, N = sum(gender), prop = gender/N)

would add the sample size and proportions of males and females in each
location. You could then subset one of the genders and use that data
frame as input to a graphics package such as ggplot2. I don't know how
you planned on plotting your data, but you can use maps in ggplot2
with a bit of care, and it is possible to plot points at different
locations of a map (e.g., lat-long coordinates) either inside ggplot2
or with the ggmaps package.

If you insist on bars/pies per location, the ggsubplot package might
be helpful.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
If you have only two or a few groups, many of us would use faceting, e.g.
print(ggplot(g,aes(gender))+geom_bar()+facet_grid(group~.))

For a lot of groups, as Dennis said plyr is a powerful option. A
simple loop-based alternative to plot gender ratios would look like
this:
for( i in unique(g$group)) {
 df <- subset(g,group==i)
 p <- ggplot(df, aes(gender) ) + geom_bar() + ggtitle(i)
 print(p)
 ggsave(paste0(i,".pdf")) # if you want to save plots
}

Ben

messages.subject: Re: jitter error
messages.body_plain:
Hi, this basically is what Murphy's says: but here are some examples of what might go wrong and how to fix it when combining box plots and a jittered geom_point plot:

# load library
library(ggplot2)

# draw a boxplot with '+' symbol for outliers
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(cyl), mpg))
p1 <- p + geom_boxplot(outlier.shape=3)
p1

# overlay with points (with horizontal jitter)
p1 + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width=0.2))
# this indeed provides duplicate outlier points

# fix duplicates, by not showing outliers in initial boxplot
p2 <- p + geom_boxplot(outlier.colour=NA)
p2 + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width=0.2))

# overlay boxplots on geom_points: points or obscured
p3 <- p + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width=0.2))
p3 +  geom_boxplot(outlier.colour=NA)

# remove fill of box plots to uncover obscured points:
p3 + geom_boxplot(outlier.colour=NA, fill = NA)

Best,

Richard

messages.body_plain:
On Thu, Feb 27, 2014 at 12:20 PM, Lorenzo Isella
<lorenzo...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Apologies for posting this to two different mailing lists, but I really need
> some cross expertise.
> I am trying to do the following: plot a geographical map colored according
> to a scalar value (choropleth map) and to overimpose a network on the map.
> To fix the ideas, you can imagine that I am plotting the GDP in different
> countries (choropleth map) and the flow of payments among them (here is
> where the network kicks in).

The code at the end of the email is a little too long for me to test
it but as long as your map data is in lat lon, it should to be
difficult to do what you want, and keep everything in lat lon.

Basically you need

map_data <- read.shp(...)
map_data <- fortify(map_data)

network_data <- read.table(...)

# now both map_data and network_data have columns lat and lon
# the question is really how your network data is formated. The
best/easiest would be with 5 columns: startLon, startLat, endLon,
endLat, amount

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(aes(x=lon, y=lat, fill=...), data=map_data) +
  geom_segment(aes(x=startLon, y=startLat, xend=endLon, yend=endLat,
size=amount), data=network_data)

messages.subject: Re: average dashline
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, Mar 4, 2014 at 10:53 PM, J H <renalcl...@gmail.com> wrote:
> in the ggplot2 boxplot the median gets calculated, but how about mean.  what
> is the best way to add it?  I prefer ggplot2 to calculate it.  I know
> geom_vline or hline adds it if I bring the data in, but preference would be
> for R do it based on how my x axis is separated.  Thanks.

You would need to write a new stat_* function that works as
stat_boxplot (i.e. outputs the same values in a data.frame, see
?stat_boxplot).

*But* this is probably a bad idea. Boxplots are not just defined by
their visual aspect, the fact that the central line is the median, the
whiskers extend to 1.5 * the interquartile range etc. all participate
in the definition of what a botplot is. So by making a non-standard
boxplot, you will be confusing your readers. I would advise you to
create a new, different looking plot altogether if you want to show
the mean instead of the median.

messages.subject: Re: Facet with Multiple Span Parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

As Ben mentioned, you want to save the individual ggplots to separate
objects. You can use the grid.arrange() function in the gridExtra
package to plot them in sequence.

Starting with your code,

require(ggplot2)
x <- runif(100,min=-4*pi, max=4*pi)
df <- data.frame(x=x,y=sin(x))

p1 <- qplot(df$x, df$y)+stat_smooth(span=.4) + ggtitle(span = 0.4)
p2 <- qplot(df$x, df$y)+stat_smooth(span=.5) + ggtitle(span = 0.5)
p3 <- qplot(df$x, df$y)+stat_smooth(span=.6) + ggtitle(span = 0.6)
p4 <- qplot(df$x, df$y)+stat_smooth(span=.7) + ggtitle(span = 0.7)

library(gridExtra)
grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, p4, ncol = 2)

A more efficient way to do this (using the DRY principle) is to write
a function to do each plot with a variable span, save the plots as a
list and then use grid.arrange(). Here's one way; I changed the data
frame name to avoid potential conflicts with the df() function.

DF <- data.frame(x=x, y=sin(x))

# Function to draw a single loess smooth; span is its formal argument
plotfun <- function(span = 0.5)
{
   require(ggplot2)
   ggplot(DF, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
       geom_point() +
       stat_smooth(span = span) +
       ggtitle(paste0("span = ", span))
}

# Produce a vector of spans
spans <- seq(0.4, 0.7, by = 0.1)

# Use the lapply function to recursively call plotfun() with different spans
plots <- lapply(spans, function(x) plotfun(x))

require(gridExtra)
# use the do.call() function to invoke grid.arrange() since the plots
are in a list
suppressMessages(do.call(grid.arrange, plots))

BTW:  DRY = "Don't Repeat Yourself", in case you didn't already know that.
Dennis

In the absence of a reproducible example:

You mean something like this?

set.seed(357)
div.trip <- data.frame(
  day = factor(rep(c("mon", "tue", "wed", "thu", "fri", "sat", "sun"), 4),
               levels = c("mon", "tue", "wed", "thu", "fri", "sat", "sun")),
  gender = rep(c("male", "female"), each = 14),
  group = rep(c("control", "treatment"), times = 14),
  count = c(40 + rnorm(n = 14, sd = 3), 35 + rnorm(n = 14, sd = 2)))

subset(div.trip, day == "mon")

ggplot(div.trip, aes(x = day, y = count, color = gender)) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_line(aes(group = gender)) +
  facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 1)

Cheers,
Roman

messages.body_plain:
Numbers we generate (using e.g. rnorn()) are generated almost at random -- they're pseudo random. There's a formula behind the generation, and this formula repeats these numbers in periods over and over again. The period is luckily quite large (default PRNG is 2^19937 - 1). If you want your code to be fully reproducible, you can include a specific start of this period, so that all the numbers will match (and they will still be pseudo random). This is handy when you're working on simulations and you want your work to be faithfully reproduced.

In practice this means that the graph you saw when you first ran the code, looks exactly the same the way I made it. I don't like to make up stuff (hardest part is naming variables), so I usually use 357 as a start of PRNG, which happens to be my favorite caliber. :)

HTH,
Roman

messages.subject: Re: geom_jitter mystery- Please help
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Thank you for providing data and code. I named your data DF to avoid potential conflicts with the table() function.

Problem 1:

require(ggplot2)
ggplot(DF, aes(x=State, y=Sales, fill=State)) +
   geom_boxplot(outlier.colour = NA) +
   geom_jitter(position=position_jitter(width=0.1), size=4, alpha=0.3)

Problem 2:

ggplot(DF, aes(x=State, y=Sales2, fill=State)) +
   geom_boxplot()  +
   geom_jitter(position=position_jitter(width=0.1, height = 0), size=4, alpha=0.3)

In the first problem, setting outlier.colour = NA (and you do need the Commonwealth spelling) effectively removes the boxplot points from being displayed. In the second problem, you controlled the width of the jitter but not the height. Setting height = 0 jitters points horizontally with width 0.1.

Dennis

On Thu, Mar 6, 2014 at 3:38 PM, J H <renalcl...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Dennis,

All the Sales2 values were zero. When you specify geom_point(), ggplot2 will plot points. It just does what you ask it to do.

> If I just use the code geom_jitter() I still get the same problem with R even though values are true zero's.

Which problem? Code example??

> Am I  missing something? would using height=0 artificially suppress any true >0 values?

Jittering can occur both vertically and horizontally. My code suppressed the vertical jitter but left the horizontal jitter, which is why you got a pseudo-rug plot at the median of each box plot. If you had nonzero values, specifying height = 0 in geom_jitter() or position_jitter() will suppress any vertical jittering of the points, but nonzero values would still be plotted with some horizontal jitter unless you remove the jittering altogether, in which case you'll get one value plotted for Sales2 in each group at zero.

The reason your original code plotted points away from zero when Sales2 was the response is because you allowed both horizontal and vertical jitter; see ?geom_jitter for the default values.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: legends question
messages.body_plain:
If you used a line plot instead of a bar chart, this would be fairly
easy: map color in each layer to a named factor level and use
scale_color_manual() to set the colors. For example,

qplot(data=allqueriesDF,
        x = as.Date(Date),
        y = Queries,
        xlab = "Date",
        ylab = "Queries") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
    theme_bw() +

    geom_line(aes(color = "All queries"), size = 2) +
    geom_line(data=spamqueriesDF,
        aes(x=as.Date(Date), y=Queries,
            color = "Spam queries"), size=2) +
    geom_line(data=allqueriesDF,
        aes(x=as.Date(Date), y=mean(Queries),
            color = "Mean"), size=2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("blue", "red", "goldenrod")) +
    labs(color = "Type")

If you insist on keeping the bar chart, you have a problem because
blue is set to fill whereas red and goldenrod are set to color. You
could use blue for the color aesthetic in the bar chart and then it
would work by substituting the aes(color = "All queries") part into

messages.subject: Re: regression line with eq
messages.body_plain:
Here's a Q & D way to do it - I named your data DF to avoid any conflicts with commonly occurring functions:

m <- lm(Sales2 ~ Sales1, data = DF)
mc <- round(coef(m), 2)
strg <- paste0("hat(y) == ",mc[1], " + ", mc[2], "~Sales1")

require(ggplot2)
ggplot(DF, aes(x = Sales1, y = Sales2)) +
    geom_point(size=3) +
    stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
    geom_text( x = 200, y = 2400,
              label = strg, parse = TRUE)

For textual annotation in ggplot2, the plotmath expression has to be expressed as a character string, and this needs to be done outside of ggplot2. So the game is to fit the model, extract the coefficients and then use a paste function to construct a string representation of the plotmath expression. In geom_text(), set the coordinates at which the equation should be plotted, use the name of the string as the value of the label argument and declare parse = TRUE, which will parse and evaluate the string inside ggplot2. If you want to do this for each of several panels, see here:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/ggplot2/H4Gd8c10GN4

Dennis

messages.subject: unrecognizable colors
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, I'm starting with ggplot and I can't solve this (apparently simple) problem. I'm using a sample of survey data (eph100) where P47T is individual income. The syntax

 qplot(P47T, data = eph100, colour="Red", binwidth=500)

 puts red borders, but

 qplot(P47T, data = eph100, colour="Blue", binwidth=500)

 does the same: red borders.

When I want to fill the rectangles:

 qplot(P47T, data = eph100, fill="Blue", binwidth=500)

The areas are filled with red!!

After reading answers to Ben’s question (superman emblem) I suppose this red is the default color for misinterpretations.

This syntax:

qplot(P47T, data = eph100, color="Green", fill="Blue", binwidth=500)

returns a completely red histogram (borders and filling), with a legend that identifies the names of colors with different colors. It seems that R is considering new objects called green and blue, but if I eliminate the quotation marks, results in an error, because R says: “object 'Green' not found”

The numbers from the color chart neither work:

qplot(P47T, data = eph100, color=257, fill=490, binwidth=500)

gives a completely blue histogram, the same with any number combination.

Can anybody help?

Thanks

>

  You need to protect explicit values (rather than mappings) with I()
when using qplot, e.g.

 qplot(P47T, data = eph100, colour=I("Red"), binwidth=500)

 and similarly for fill etc.

Are these the objectives? Relabeling fill variable levels in legend and second, reordering sequence of legend levels.

1. Relabeling (see Winston Chang's cookbook site: http://www.cookbook-r.com/Graphs/Legends_(ggplot2)/)
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(TEMP, aes(x=CiradMed, Nbre)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = Type), stat="identity", width = 0.7)
######################################

q=p +

  facet_wrap(~ Annee,nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Tout type de publication",     #titre graphique
    y = "Pourcentage de publications",  #label axe y
    fill="Type de\npublications"  ) +       #titre legende
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size=8,colour="black",face="bold"),
    #label graduation axe x
    axis.title.x = element_blank())#suppression label axe x

q
q+ scale_fill_discrete(labels=c("A", "B", "C","E"))

2. Changing sequence of legend labels - Could be done by reordering factor levels of the fill variable.
str(TEMP)
# tells us that the fill variable, Type, is chr
levels(as.factor(TEMP$Type))# gives the default alpha ordering of CL,FI,OCO,SL
#Two steps...
# Convert Type to factor var
TEMP$Type=as.factor(TEMP$Type)
# Reordering factor levels to FI,CL,SL,OCO by specifying level numbers
TEMP$Type = factor(TEMP$Type,levels(TEMP$Type)[c(2,1,4,3)])
levels(TEMP$Type)# confirm the change

# Plot again

p <- ggplot(TEMP, aes(x=CiradMed, Nbre)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = Type), stat="identity", width = 0.7)
######################################

q=p +

  facet_wrap(~ Annee,nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Tout type de publication",     #titre graphique
    y = "Pourcentage de publications",  #label axe y
    fill="Type de\npublications"  ) +       #titre legende
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size=8,colour="black",face="bold"),
    #label graduation axe x
    axis.title.x = element_blank())#suppression label axe x

q
q+ scale_fill_discrete(labels=c("B", "A", "E","C")) # Relabeling factor levels

Best,
Vivek

messages.subject: Re: Vertical line at a date
messages.body_plain:
Evidently, even though your dates use a Microsoft Excel origin, when
plotting in ggplot2 with a Date axis, you need to use R's date origin
of 1 Jan 1970, and you need to use the numeric value of the date from
that origin for annotation such as vlines or text. The following gives
you vertical lines in each panel at the same date.

Date <- 33817:34016
y1 <- runif(200,20,200)
y2 <- rnorm(200)

library(scales)
library(ggplot2)
library(reshape2)

df <- data.frame(y1,y2,Date)
dfmelt=melt(df,id="Date")
dfmelt$Date = as.Date(dfmelt$Date, origin=('1899-12-30'))

# 8293 days from 1970-01-01 to 1992-09-15
ggplot(dfmelt,aes(x=Date,y=value))+
      geom_vline(xintercept = 8293, size = 1,
                 linetype = "dashed", color = "darkorange") +
      geom_point()+
      facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", ncol=1)+

      theme(axis.title.y = element_blank())+
      scale_x_date(labels = date_format("%m-%Y"))

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: modify the label of the legend and respect the order of colors of legend and chart
messages.subject_clean: modify the label of the legend and respect the order of colors of legend and chart
messages.body_plain:
Michel,

Apologies for the delay in replying back. My earlier suggestion for just relabeling involved introducing scale_fill_discrete(labels=...) and reordering legend labels involved reordering the factor variables and then relabeling. A much more simpler and direct  approach for reordering of labels could involve using scale_fill_discrete(breaks=...,labels=...), as in the following.

1. Use your original data: TEMP
2. Relabeling only (Unchanged from earlier suggestion)
---------------------------
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(TEMP, aes(x=CiradMed, Nbre)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = Type), stat="identity", width = 0.7)
######################################

q=p +

  facet_wrap(~ Annee,nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Tout type de publication",     #titre graphique
    y = "Pourcentage de publications",  #label axe y
    fill="Type de\npublications"  ) +       #titre legende
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size=8,colour="black",face="bold"),
    #label graduation axe x

    axis.title.x = element_blank())#suppression label axe x

q
q+ scale_fill_discrete(labels=c("A", "B", "C","E"))

-----------------------------------
3. Changing sequence of labels and relabeling
------------------------------------------------------------------
q+scale_fill_discrete(breaks=c("FI","CL","SL","OCO"),labels=c("B", "A", "E","C"))
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Few links that helped me when I faced with a similar issue in the past:
http://www.cookbook-r.com/Graphs/Legends_(ggplot2)/
https://kohske.wordpress.com/2010/12/29/faq-how-to-order-the-factor-variables-in-ggplot2/
http://learnr.wordpress.com/2010/03/23/ggplot2-changing-the-default-order-of-legend-labels-and-stacking-of-data/
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/9577680/r-sort-legend-in-ggplot2
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/7556320/reorder-legend-without-changing-order-of-points-on-plot

Best,
Vivek

messages.subject: Re: datapoints shape & color
messages.body_plain:
It's not obvious to me what you want, but if you want to group your
taxa and identify them with different shapes, here's one way you might
do it, which puts all of the groups on one plot.

ggplot(dotAW, aes(x = AASW, y = WW)) +
    geom_point(aes(shape = shape),
               position = position_jitter(width = 0.005, height = 0.005)) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(1, 0, 2),
                       labels = c("Group 1", "Group 2", "Group 3")) +
    labs(shape = "Taxa\ngroups")

I had no idea how you wanted to name the subgroups, so I just threw
something out there; edit it to something sensible.

Another option is to facet by taxa subgroups. If you want to do this,
I'd change the values in dotAW$shape to something more relevant as the
values become the strip titles in the faceted plot.

ggplot(dotAW, aes(x = AASW, y = WW)) +
    geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.005, height = 0.005)) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1) + facet_wrap(~ shape, nrow = 1)

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ggplot Community,

I have a similar problem as explained in the thread below.
I would like to plot several interaction effects across groups, based on regression coefficients and intercepts that I get from previous analysis. I can plot it by default. However, I want to generalize the script via a function and that doesn't really seem to work.
Could you maybe help me figure out where I am going wrong? Or which loophole I am not aware of?

Here's a (hopefully) reproducible snippet. My aim is to get identical graphs for concrete.graph and gen.graph.

Thanks a lot for your input!

##'Defining the objects
rm<-data.frame(x=1:5,1000,replace=T)
rm$y<-rm$x*4+4
beta.df<-data.frame(group=c(1,2,3), intercept=c(0.35,0.37,0.5),m3=c(0.2,0.35,0.3))
col<-c("red","blue","green")

#Effects for 3 groups
poly1r <- function(x) {beta.df$intercept[1]+beta.df$m3[1]*x}
poly2r <- function(x) {beta.df$intercept[2]+beta.df$m3[2]*x}
poly3r <- function(x) {beta.df$intercept[3]+beta.df$m3[3]*x}

concrete.graph<-ggplot(rm,aes(x=x))
concrete.graph<-concrete.graph+stat_function(fun = poly1r, colour="black", size=2)
concrete.graph<-concrete.graph+stat_function(fun = poly2r, colour="red", size=2)
concrete.graph<-concrete.graph+stat_function(fun = poly3r, colour="blue", size=2)
concrete.graph

###Generalized function (for n groups)
mini.graph<- function (n) {
graph<-ggplot(relmo,aes(x=rel))
for (g in 1:n) {
polyr <- function(x) {beta.df$intercept[g]+beta.df$m3[g]*x}
graph<-graph+stat_function(fun = polyr, colour=col[g], size=2)
}
return(graph)
}

gen.graph<-mini.graph(3)

ggplot(newdf, aes(x = factor(Sex), fill = factor(Group), y = score)) +

My actual data I'm trying to do this with has many, many dots in the dotplot and some IDs go up and others go down.   I really like the dotplot for this presentation purpose, so would ideally have a solution using geom_dotplot

Many thanks

James Curley

messages.subject: Re: scale_colour_gradient and na.value
messages.body_plain:
On 3/13/2014 9:44 AM, Stevan Lauriault wrote:
> Hi,
>
> Trying to generate two NA.value colours in scale_colour-gradient.. one for
> points that fall below the lower limit (green), one for points that fall
> above the lower limit (red).
>
> Something like:
>
> clr<-x[,i]
> plt<-qplot(main=main, colnames(x[i]), sep=""), x[,1], x[,2], data=x,
> colour=clr) +
> scale_colour_gradient(low="green", high="red", space="Lab",
> limits=c(low,high), na.value = c("green","red"))

Change the scale call to:

scale_colour_gradient(low = "green", high = "red", space = "Lab",
                       limits=c(low, high), oob = squish)

squish takes anything outside the limits and pushes it to the edge of
the limits, which is exactly what you want. (I'll admit, this
possibility/behavior isn't obvious from the documentation.)

The reason your previous attempt didn't work is that there is really
only one NA value, and there is no distinction between NA from being too
high vs NA from being too low.

> but it doesn't work.  Any developments here?
>
> thx,
>
> Steve
>

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: Re: datapoints shape & color
messages.body_plain:
Just add a color aesthetic, but you probably want to merge the two
legends so you have to make sure they have the same breaks, labels and
legend titles.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(dotAW, aes(x = AASW, y = WW)) +

#    theme_bw() +
    geom_point(aes(shape = shape, color = shape),

               position = position_jitter(width = 0.005, height = 0.005)) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1) +

    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1",

                       labels = c("Group 1", "Group 2", "Group 3")) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(1, 0, 2),
                       labels = c("Group 1", "Group 2", "Group 3")) +

    labs(shape = "Taxa\ngroups", color = "Taxa\ngroups")

This doesn't seem like an improvement to me; to make the colors stand
out, it's probably better to use solid shapes rather than hollow ones,
but the tradeoff is more visual clutter and obscurity in the lower
left corner of the plot.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I like the plot you generated, since it's visually less cluttered and
you can still compare male-female differences side-by-side.

You can, however, put the two of them together by removing
facet_grid(). With a couple of cosmetic changes:

newdf <- data.frame(ID = c("aa", "ab", "ac", "ad", "ae", "af"),

                    Sex=rep(c("male", "female"), 6),

                    Group = rep(c("old", "new"), each = 6),
                    score = 12:1)

ggplot(newdf, aes(x=Group, y=score)) +
  geom_path(aes(color = Sex, group = ID), size = 1) +
  geom_dotplot(aes(fill = Sex), binaxis="y", binwidth = .5,stackdir =
"centerwhole") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("orange", "blue")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("orange", "blue"))

The last two lines give you control over the rendered colors.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Firstly, your example is not reproducible because 'fits' wasn't
supplied, so there is no frame of reference for someone to diagnose
the problem exactly.

On Thu, Mar 13, 2014 at 3:08 PM, yosts <yo...@mindspring.com> wrote:
> Here's my code in a function called from elsewhere:
>
> plot.polyreg <- function(fits)  {
>
>   library(ggplot2)
>   maxdeg <- length(fits) - 2

length() is normally used to indicate the number of elements of an
atomic object. If you use it in a data frame, it returns the number of
columns. The safer (and more understandable) code is ncol(fits) if
fits is indeed a data frame.
>
> dfits <- data.frame(fits$x, fits$y)

The above suggests that fits has more than one component, which means
it could be a data frame or a list.

> aa <- fits$x
> bb <- fits$y

aa and bb are repetitious and unnecessary here. The next line can be called with

gggp <- qplot(x = x, y = y, data = dfits, geom = "point")

> ggqp <- qplot(x=fits$x, y=fits$y, data=dfits, geom = "point")
> print(ggqp)
> print(aa)
> print(bb)
>

Again, when the data frame is named, you don't need to call it again
to access the variables:

ggp <- ggplot(dfits, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point()

And here's the problem; you call the data frame dfits, and then try to
access fits$x and fits$y, which reside in a different object. If you
use the above line (and it reflects what you want), the problem should
disappear.

> ggp <- ggplot(dfits, aes(x=fits$x, y=fits$y)) + geom_point()

I don't know the purpose of this next line...

> summary(ggp)
> ggp <- ggp + xlab("XX") + ylab("YY")
>

After you fix the above line of code, this should work..

> print(ggp)                     #This seems to blow its mind.
>
> .
> .
> }
>

> The qplot works, all the print and summary statements work, down to the
> print(ggp).  Upon execution of the print(ggp), it tells me in the debugger
> in the console window
> that it can't find any object, and the plot is blank:
>

The error message in the first line is informative:

> Browse[2]> plot(ggp)
> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'fits' not found
> Called from: top level
> Browse[3]> summary(ggqp)
> Error during wrapup: object 'ggqp' not found
> Browse[3]> aa
> Error during wrapup: object 'aa' not found
> Browse[3]> bb
> Error during wrapup: object 'bb' not found
> Browse[3]> maxdeg
> Error during wrapup: object 'maxdeg' not found
> Browse[3]> ggp
> Error during wrapup: object 'ggp' not found
>
> I am using RStudio.  In the "data values" window, all these objects appear
> fine. All have the right values.  But the code can't find anything.

It's hard to tell what type of object fits is supposed to be, but if
it's a data frame, try something like this:

plot.polyreg <- function(fits)  {

  require(ggplot2)
  maxdeg <- ncol(fits) - 2

# If fits is a data frame, the next line may be unnecessary
# dfits <- data.frame(fits$x, fits$y)
ggqp <- qplot(x=x, y=y, data=dfits, geom = "point")
print(ggqp)
print(dfits)

ggp <- ggplot(dfits, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point()

ggp <- ggp + xlab("XX") + ylab("YY")

print(ggp)

.
.
.
}

Suggestion: simplify the function as much as possible. When it works,
then you can start adding other things to it. That way, if something
goes wrong, you know which code you can eliminate as potentially
problematic.

Dennis

PS: When you subscribe to a mailing list, you get posts that are not
your own as well; that's part of the subscription.

messages.subject: Re: Write the values of a variable on a stacked geom_bar
messages.subject_clean: Write the values of a variable on a stacked geom_bar
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This topic is covered in Winston Chang's R Graphics Cookbook (section
3.9). Basically, you have to take a cumulative sum of the frequencies
within a given stack and then subtract off half the frequency in each
'sub-bin' (for lack of a better term). Using the plyr package, here's
one way to reformat the data and produce the plot.

library(plyr)

# Cumulate Nbre by combinations of the three factors
tfreq <- count(TEMP, c("Annee", "CiradMed", "Type"), wt_var = "Nbre")

# The variable cfreq is what you want to use to position the labels
# in the y-direction
tfreq <- ddply(tfreq, .(Annee, CiradMed), mutate,
                 cfreq = cumsum(freq) - 0.5 * freq)

ggplot(tfreq, aes(x=CiradMed, y = freq)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = Type), stat = "identity",
            position = "stack", width = 0.7) +

  facet_wrap(~ Annee,nrow = 1) +
  labs(y = "Pourcentage")  +                      #label axe y
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill='white', colour='white'),
    panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA, color = "black"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size=8,colour="black",face="bold"),

    axis.title.x = element_blank())  + #suppression label axe x
  geom_text(aes(y = cfreq, label = freq), size = 4)

Dennis

messages.subject: How to create a facetted plot from a list of S4 objects
messages.subject_clean: How to create a facetted plot from a list of S4 objects
messages.body_plain:
Ok, this is somewhat involved, but I'm hoping someone can help me. I have a list of S4 objects returned from the {changepoint} package. This package determines changes in mean along a time-series. I applied the change point function to a data frame, by a factor corresponding two each sample time-series, which returned this list of S4 objects. The changepoint package has a very nifty plot function to plot these objects and I've provided a .png to show what I'm hoping to achieve for one graph. I'd like to use ggplot2 though. I'm including a dput() of one of the S4 objects in the list as a text file.

I'd like to end up with a facetted plot, with each facet corresponding to an S4 object. The plots themselves would have the time series values on the y-axis, overlaid by the changepoint means using geom_segment().

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Thanks for the example data. You can't use the S4 object directly in
ggplot2; ggplot(), in particular, requires a data frame for input so I
converted everything to that.

Two data frames were created, basically by copying/pasting pieces of
the S4 object:
   - tsdat, in which I formed a data frame out of the time series
index and its values (data.set);
   - chgpts, in which the slot cpts was broken down into two vectors,
start and end, along with the predicted changepoint means. start and
end refer to the x-endpoints for each segment.
>From those, the plot was pretty straightforward to create.

cpts = c(14L, 175L, 261L, 283L, 772L, 908L)
mean = c(0.725140037285714, 0.732281273099379,0.728254444453488,
   0.721260706636364, 0.713166732728016, 0.709311015801471)
chgpts <- data.frame(start = c(0, cpts[-length(cpts)]), end = cpts, yhat = mean)

# Using the attachment,
tsdat <- dget("tsdat.R")
# tsdat <- data.frame(time = seq_along(data.set), y = as.numeric(data.set))

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(data = tsdat, aes(x = time, y = y)) +
    geom_path() +
    geom_segment(data = chgpts,
                 aes(x = start, xend = end, y = yhat, yend = yhat),
                 color = "red", size = 1)

I don't work much with S4 objects and didn't know how to read your
attachment into an R object, but it wasn't hard to pick out the
pieces. There's probably an easier way to reformat your data. OTOH,
this gives you an idea of what you need to pass into ggplot() to
reproduce your graph.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Disease mapping using ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Here's one way you could do it with the ggmap package. Note that there
are several ways to download maps in ggmap and several ways to render
them, so if you want something different, use this as a template to
get started and modify to your tastes.

# sidra <- read.csv("sidra.csv", header = TRUE)

# Attach a few packages to the session
library(reshape2)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggmap)

# Idea here is to stack the observed and expected counts
# to make it easier to plot the two together in ggplot2
sidram <- melt(sidra, measure = c("Observed", "Expected"))

# This is one way to get a map of the region from ggmap via GoogleEarth
# If you want something different, one choice is to change the maptype
# argument. If you want an administrative map of the area, that's a
# completely different problem; see gadm.org <http://gadm.org> for that.
mapImage <- get_map(location = c(lon = 73.13, lat = 31.35),
               source = "google",
               maptype = 'satellite',
               zoom = 10)

# Plot the map and the points; since the area is not familiar to me,
# I added the town names at the end. The mapped vjust and hjust
# values are designed to spread out the positions of the names on the map.
# You can change the colors if you don't like them - I used pink and black
# because they have high contrast and you can see the relative size
# of the differences rather easily.
ggmap(mapImage,
    extent = "device",
    legend = "topleft",
    ylab = "Latitude",
    xlab = "Longitude") +
  geom_point(data = sidram, aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude,
                               colour = variable, size = value)) +
  scale_size_area() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("pink", "black")) +
  geom_text(data = sidra, aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, label = X,
                              vjust = c(-1, -1, -1, -1, 2, -1, 2, -1),
                              hjust = 0.5 + c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0.7, 0, -0.7, 0)),
               color = "yellow", size = 4)

Another option is to use maptype = "roadmap"; here's one attempt at it:

mapImage <- get_map(location = c(lon = 73.13, lat = 31.35),
               source = "google",
               maptype = 'roadmap',
               zoom = 10)
ggmap(mapImage,
    extent = "device",
    darken = c(0.8, "white")) +
  geom_point(data = sidram, aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude,
                               colour = variable, size = value)) +
  scale_size_area() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("navy", "yellow"))  +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.15, 0.85))

The darken = option in ggmap() allows you to put the roadmap more in
the background of the plot so that the points stand out.

These are not the only options you have, so look into the ggmap
package, which has a number of interesting examples in its help pages.

Dennis

Hi:

This is just something to get you started - you probably want a wider
range of colors than what is shown here. I used scale_fill_gradient2()
below; see its on-line help page for more information:
http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/scale_gradient2.html

You might also consider looking into colorRampPalette() or the
colorspace package for more options with scale_gradientn(). There are
several examples in Hadley's ggplot2 book that show how to define a
palette for use in a suitable scale_gradient*() function. (BTW, greens
and reds are not good choices for color palettes - see the help page
above for an explanation why.

#-----

TEMP <- structure(list(Annee = c("2004", "2005", "2006", "2007", "2008",
"2009", "2010", "2011", "2012", "2013"), Nbre = c(877L, 944L,
946L, 984L, 1238L, 1201L, 1256L, 1217L, 1349L, 1158L)), .Names = c("Annee",
"Nbre"), row.names = c(NA, -10L), class = "data.frame")

TEMP$Annee <- factor(TEMP$Annee)

library(ggplot2)
# avec ggplot
ggplot(TEMP, aes(x=Annee, y=Nbre)) +

geom_bar(aes(fill = Nbre), stat="identity", width = 0.7) +
   scale_fill_gradient2(high = "darkgreen", low = "greenyellow", mid = "green")
#----

Dennis

a<-"ggplot(data=rm,aes(x=x))+\n"

}

messages.subject: missing legend
messages.body_plain:
Dear ggplotters,

I am trying to realize plots with a legend explaining all 8 lines plotted in each sector of the plotting area:
I have 4 variables (Variable, Type, Year, and the value Moran.I) and I want all Type(=1:8) plotted in the same plot. Somehow the legend does not appear.

Any help on the issue is very much appreciated!

Ale

# Factor definition
MoranI$layer1 <- factor(MoranI$Type)

p <- ggplot(MoranI, aes(Year,Moran.I))

p <- p + geom_point(data=MoranI[which(MoranI$Type=="1"),],colour = "red",linetype=1, size = 1) +
  geom_line(data=MoranI[which(MoranI$Type=="2"),],colour = "red",linetype=2,  size = 1)  +
  geom_line(data=MoranI[which(MoranI$Type=="3"),],colour = "black",linetype=1,  size = 1)  +
  geom_line(data=MoranI[which(MoranI$Type=="4"),],colour = "black",linetype=2,  size = 1)  +
  geom_line(data=MoranI[which(MoranI$Type=="5"),],colour = "black",linetype=3,  size = 1)  +
  geom_line(data=MoranI[which(MoranI$Type=="6"),],colour = "blue", linetype=1, size = 1)  +
  geom_line(data=MoranI[which(MoranI$Type=="7"),],colour = "blue", linetype=2, size = 1)  +
  geom_line(data=MoranI[which(MoranI$Type=="8"),],colour = "blue",linetype=3,  size = 1)  +
  labs(title = "Moran's I",
       x = "", y = "") +
   scale_fill_manual(values=c("red", "red", "black", "black", "black", "blue", "blue", "blue"),
                             labels=c("First Order Queen", "Rook", "20km","50km","100km","5 Nearest Neigh.","10 Nearest Neigh.","15 Nearest Neigh."))    +
  facet_wrap(~ layer2)
p

Ben

You could do this:

newdf <- data.frame(x=c(3, 1, 10, 8, 63, 8, 82, 38, 6, 4, 7, 4),
    y=c(1, 2.05, 3.4, 1.9, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 2.5, 1.8, 2, 1.8))

library(ggplot2)
(g0 <- ggplot(newdf, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point())
g0 + geom_smooth(method="lm",formula=y~log(x))

  That fits the model  Y ~ N(a+b*log(x),sigma^2)
which may or may not be what you want (but which looks
reasonable in this case)

                    labels = c("Group 1", "Group 2", "Group 3")) +
  labs(shape = "Taxa\ngroups", color = "Taxa\ngroups")

To reiterate from an earlier message, in order to merge scales, each
one has to have:
  * the same legend title;
  * the same breaks;
  * the same labels.
Since both scales use the same aesthetic, the breaks will be the same
so they don't have to be stated explicitly; however, the labels do
have to be stated in each scale since they differ from their defaults
(the factor levels, which in this case are circle, rectangle and
triangle). Setting the two legend titles in labs() ensures the same
legend titles.

Since you use point jittering, you need to expand your x- and y-limits
on the low end to avoid having jittered points removed from the plot.
With this specification, only the two outliers are removed from the
plot (as opposed to 13 or 14 from your last code chunk).

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Fitting a logarithmic curve to a ggplot
messages.subject_clean: Fitting a logarithmic curve to a ggplot
messages.body_plain:
In addition to Ben's reply, you have a few other options:

# Option 1: Transform x in the ggplot() call; the x-axis
#    will then be in the log scale
ggplot(newdf, aes(x = log(x), y = y)) + geom_point() +
   geom_smooth(method = lm)

# Option 2: Use the trans = option of scale_x_continuous()
ggplot(newdf, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log")

In options 1 and 2, both transform x to the log scale before computing
the axes. The difference between the two is the set of default breaks;
you can use the breaks = argument in scale_x_continuous() to define
your own.

Option 3 applies a coordinate transformation, which occurs after the
original scales have been drawn. The effect is to warp the original
scaling on the x-axis to a logarithmic one as well as the shape of the
fitted model. You can use this to see the connection between Ben's
solution and the two given above:

ggplot(newdf, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, formula = y ~ log(x)) +
  coord_trans(xtrans = "log")

Dennis

> gg <- gg + geom_bar(stat = 'identity')  + xlab('')
Error: Don't know how to add geom_bar(stat = "identity") to a plot

Traceback shed light on the matter:
> traceback()
3: stop("Don't know how to add ", objectname, " to a plot", call. = FALSE)
2: add_ggplot(e1, e2, e2name)
1: `+.gg`(ggplot(plotDf, aes(x = xVar, y = yVar)), geom_bar())

Then I realized that ggplot itself uses 'gg' as a variable name. In fact, it is even one of the classes in ggplot2.

After replacing gg by pp, it worked!
> pp <- ggplot(plotDf, aes(x = xVar, y = yVar))
> pp <- pp + geom_bar(stat = 'identity')  + xlab('')

Just wanted to share this with others who encounter this problem in future!

Adi

messages.body_plain:
Lucy, I didn't go load the splancs package because one thing that
immediately jumps out at me is that your "Date" field is a string.
Probably the first step is to convert it to a true date, e.g.

library(lubridate)
sample$TrueDate <- dmy(paste0("01/",sample$Date))

That done, you have something you can work with:

test <- interp(sample$TrueDate,sample$y,sample$x,duplicate='mean')
filled.contour(test)

Hope this is a useful first step.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Gant Charts
messages.body_plain:
To build on Roman's geom_rect example, this Gantt-ish graph <https://github.com/LiveOak/NlsyLinksDetermination/blob/master/Publications/2013France/Graphs/Timeline.png> was created from this CSV <http://Cohort,%20Label,StartYear,StopYear,%20Offset%201,DOB,1955,1965,-1.5%202,DOB,1970,2009,-1.5%203,DOB,1980,1984,-1.5%201,Surveys,1979,2010,-0.5%202,Surveys,1986,2010,-0.5%203,Surveys,1997,2010,-0.5%201,Fertility,1970,2009,0.5%202,Fertility,1987,2010,0.5%203,Fertility,1994,2010,0.5> and this code <https://github.com/LiveOak/NlsyLinksDetermination/blob/master/Publications/2013France/Graphs/Timeline.R>.

There's a few nonstandard annotations (and a few shortcut that don't follow best practices).  The meat of the graphing code is:
ggplot(ds, aes(xmin=StartYear, xmax=StopYear, ymin=HeightMin, ymax=HeightMax, fill=Label)) +
  geom_rect(color=NA) + #The color bars of data; use just the fill
  geom_text(aes(x=Year, y=Height, label=Label), hjust=.5)

The important code that adds to the CSV is
width <- .2
ds$HeightMin <- ds$Cohort + ds$Offset*width
ds$HeightMax <- ds$HeightMin + width
ds$Height <- (ds$HeightMax + ds$HeightMin)/2
ds$Year <- (ds$StartYear + pmin(ds$StopYear, 2010))/2

messages.subject: Re: need help with contour plot
messages.body_plain:
Generally speaking, with ggplot you want all your variables in a
single data frame, and then you tell ggplot your data, aesthetic
mappings, and geom to use. So for example, in this case could do:

library(reshape)
zdf <- melt(z)
zdf <- cbind(zdf,expand.grid(1:length(x),1:length(y)))

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(zdf,aes(Var1,Var2))+geom_raster(aes(fill=value))

This basically duplicates the filled.contour output.

Ben

messages.subject: [Merging ggmap maps] 3 equal size/scale/zoom maps show different margins once merged
messages.subject_clean: [Merging ggmap maps] 3 equal size/scale/zoom maps show different margins once merged
messages.body_plain:
Hi there!,

Is there any way of fixing the plot-area size of -ggmap- function as after trying to merge two or more maps?. I have three graphs (maps) that have the same scale, zoom and geo-dimentions, i.e. all three of them were downloaded from OSM, using scale = OSM_scale_lookup(zoom = 7) and the same bounding box sizes, the only diference is on latitude coordinates, these follow:

Map1:
 left bottom  right    top
 -75    -29    -65    -16

Map2:
 left bottom  right    top
 -75    -42    -65    -29

Map3:
 left bottom  right    top
 -75    -55    -65    -42

Please note that abs(top - bottom) always equals 13, thus, considering that the three maps should have the same dimentions, I was hoping that once I merge them into a single device they all keep the same width and height (and that is where my problem lies). The code I'm using to generate this:

# left, bottom, right, top
b.box <- c(left=-75, bottom=-55, right=-65, top=-16)

# Setting boxes
tamano <- abs(b.box["top"] - b.box["bottom"])/3
b.box1 <- b.box2 <- b.box3 <- b.box
b.box1["bottom"] <- b.box1["top"] - tamano

b.box2["top"] <- b.box1["bottom"]
b.box2["bottom"] <- b.box1["bottom"] - tamano

b.box3["top"] <- b.box2["bottom"]
b.box3["bottom"] <- b.box2["bottom"] - tamano

mymap1 <- get_map(b.box1,source="osm",scale=OSM_scale_lookup(zoom =7), color="bw")
mymap2 <- get_map(b.box2,source="osm",scale=OSM_scale_lookup(zoom =7), color="bw")
mymap3 <- get_map(b.box3,source="osm",scale=OSM_scale_lookup(zoom =7), color="bw")

map1 <- ggmap(mymap1,extent="normal") + labs(title="Zona Norte")
map2 <- ggmap(mymap2,extent="normal") + labs(title="Zona Centro")
map3 <- ggmap(mymap3,extent="normal") + labs(title="Zona Sur")

# Merging
gridExtra::grid.arrange(map1, map2,map3, ncol=3)

Please note that abs(top - bottom) always equals 13, thus, considering that the three maps should have the same dimentions, I was hoping that once I merge them into a single device they all keep the same width and height (and that is where my problem lies). I have attached a picture of what I'm getting as a result after merging the three maps.

Thanks in advanced!

George

messages.subject: Re: NA value in the legend of the plot ?
messages.subject_clean: NA value in the legend of the plot ?
messages.body_plain:
There is an argument in the scale functions to plot NA values of the
aesthetic in a different color (the default is "gray50" or "grey50",
depending on your preferred spelling); however, it does not print an
entry in the legend because by default, NAs are excluded as legitimate
factor levels. If you use the 'exclude = NULL' argument in factor() to
generate an NA level, it still doesn't get passed to the legend in
ggplot2. Therefore, you need to resort to the 'replace the NA by
something else' in order to have it represented in the legend.

I went about this in a more roundabout way, but got to the same place:

msleep2 <- msleep[!is.na <http://is.na>(msleep$sleep_cycle), ]

# Recast vore as a factor with an NA level
msleep2$Vore <- as.character(msleep2$vore)
msleep2$Vore[is.na <http://is.na>(msleep2$Vore)] <- "NA"
msleep2$Vore <- factor(msleep2$Vore,  levels = c("carni", "herbi", "insecti",
                            "omni", "NA"))

qplot(sleep_total, sleep_cycle, data=msleep2, colour=Vore) +
  scale_colour_manual("que mange\nt il ?",
      values = c("firebrick", "brown", "darkorange", "dodgerblue", "black"),

      labels = c("plante", "viande", "tout", "insecte", "Ne sais pas"))

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brandon!

Thanks for the reply. Just like you, I'm having trouble to get access to OSM, so I've switched to google. Either way, I'm still getting the same problem. As google does not support bouding box, I'm trimming the maps on my own using scale_x_continuous(). The example follows (with the new result attached):

library(ggmap)
library(gridExtra)
rm(list=ls())

b.box <- c(left=-75, bottom=-55, right=-65, top=-16)

# Setting boxes
tamano <- abs(b.box["top"] - b.box["bottom"])/3
b.box1 <- b.box2 <- b.box3 <- b.box
b.box1["bottom"] <- b.box1["top"] - tamano

b.box2["top"] <- b.box1["bottom"]
b.box2["bottom"] <- b.box1["bottom"] - tamano

b.box3["top"] <- b.box2["bottom"]
b.box3["bottom"] <- b.box2["bottom"] - tamano

# Getting the centre coordinates
centre <- function(x) c(lon=(x["right"]+x["left"])/2,lat=(x["top"]+x["bottom"])/2)

mymap1 <- get_map(centre(b.box1),source="google",zoom=4, color="bw")
mymap2 <- get_map(centre(b.box2),source="google",zoom=4, color="bw")
mymap3 <- get_map(centre(b.box3),source="google",zoom=4, color="bw")

map1 <- ggmap(mymap1,extent="normal") + labs(title="Zona Norte") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits=b.box1[c("left","right")]) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=b.box1[c("bottom","top")])

map2 <- ggmap(mymap2,extent="normal") + labs(title="Zona Centro") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits=b.box2[c("left","right")]) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=b.box2[c("bottom","top")])

map3 <- ggmap(mymap3,extent="normal") + labs(title="Zona Sur") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits=b.box3[c("left","right")]) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=b.box3[c("bottom","top")])

# Merging
gridExtra::grid.arrange(map1, map2,map3, ncol=3)

Thanks!

B

messages.subject: Add geom_point to geom_boxplot
messages.body_plain:
So I have a boxplot to which I would like to add non-jittered points. However, I am plotting one factor on the boxplot and want to plot the other factor as points, but it won't let me do this. I was having trouble plotting one factor of the data set anyway, so I made a new data set with only the one factor, but that means I have to add the points from a separate data set. Does anyone have an idea of how to do this? I figured it out using the regular plot() and points() functions, but I really prefer the graphs from ggplot and would like to use those if possible. Here's what I'm trying to do in ggplot (using data sets with only the factors I want) vs. plot:

ggplot(d2, aes(x=Lordosis, y=GEO.L1.TPL, fill=Lordosis)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_point(d3, aes(x=Lordosis, y=GEO.L1.TPL))

**** Error: ggplot2 doesn't know how to deal with data of class uneval

WORKING:

plot(d$GEO.L1.TPL[d$Species=="Human"] ~ d$Lordosis[d$Species=="Human"])

points(d$GEO.L1.TPL[d$Species=="Neandertal"] ~ d$Lordosis[d$Species=="Neandertal"], col="black", pch=2, cex=1.3)

Any help would be greatly appreciated!!
Maria

messages.body_plain:
Here's a reproducible example in the sense that Ben mentioned.

# Fake data frame: gp is a factor, y is numeric
DF <- data.frame(gp = sample(LETTERS[1:3], 100, replace = TRUE),
                  y = rnorm(100))

library(ggplot2)

# boxplot plus strip plot, no jittering
# alpha transparency mutes the box fill color
ggplot(DF, aes(x = gp, y = y)) +
   geom_boxplot(aes(fill = gp), alpha = 0.4) +
   geom_point(size = 2.5)

# boxplot plus strip plot with controlled jittering - for this to
# work, the outside points in the boxplot need to be hidden,
# hence outlier.colour = NA (and you need that particular
# spelling)
ggplot(DF, aes(x = gp, y = y)) +
   geom_boxplot(aes(fill = gp), outlier.colour = NA, alpha = 0.4) +
   geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0.05),
              size = 2.5)

Dennis

Hey Brandon, George –

Looking briefly into the problem, it looks like you can get what you want, George, with a simple change to ggmap:::stitch.  (You just need to remove the lines order <- ... and the next one, tiles <- tiles[order].

Actually, the question helped me to realize a change in some Stamen maps stuff.  If you install the dev version I just pushed to github, you can get what you want all in one go (I think) :

install_github("ggmap", "dkahle")
library(ggmap)

# left, bottom, right, top
b.box <- c(left=-75, bottom=-55, right=-65, top=-16)

ggmap(get_stamenmap(b.box, zoom = 5, maptype = "toner"), extent = "device")
ggmap(get_stamenmap(b.box, zoom = 5, maptype = "toner-lite"), extent = "device")

b.box <- c(left=-80, bottom=-55, right=-60, top=-16)
ggmap(get_stamenmap(b.box, zoom = 5, maptype = "toner"), extent = "device")
ggmap(get_stamenmap(b.box, zoom = 5, maptype = "toner-lite"), extent = "device")

b.box <- c(left=-80, bottom=-55, right=-60, top=-16)
ggmap(get_stamenmap(b.box, zoom = 6, maptype = "toner"), extent = "device")
ggmap(get_stamenmap(b.box, zoom = 6, maptype = "toner-lite"), extent = "device")

Note that not all the Stamen maps cover the entire globe.

Cheers
david.

messages.subject_clean: Create multiple (separate) plots in one session
messages.body_plain:
I have a situation in which I have to produce 15 or 20 graphs for each
of several datasets.  The commands are the same each time; only the data
differs.  What I've been doing is to copy the commands for each plot
into R, copying the result as a bmp, pasting that into a MS word file,
removing that plot and creating the next one.  This gets tedious.

Is there a way by which I could paste the commands for all the plots
into R, and have them all be available on my screen?  That doesn't seem
to be happening now.  If I copy commands to create multiple plots, only
the last one shows up.
Thanks for any help.
David

Plot them all using an RStudio R session. The "Plots" tab keeps all plots in a session and you can use the arrows to cycle through each of them.
Use `ggsave` to write them to disk, then use your OS to cycle through them. For example, on a Mac, use Quickview.

Cheers,
Doug

messages.subject: Re: Create multiple (separate) plots in one session
messages.subject_clean: Create multiple (separate) plots in one session
messages.body_plain:
Here are a couple more suggestions (in addition to Doug's).

You can send a plot directly to a file using functions like pdf,
bitmap, png, jpeg, tif, bmp, etc.  With the bmp and other bitmap based
functions you can specify a filename that will increment with each
plot.  For example if you do bmp(filename='myplots%03d.bmp') then the
first plot will go into a file named myplots001.bmp, the second plot
will go into the file myplots002.bmp, and so forth.  Just remember to
do a dev.off() after the last plot to finalize the last file.  This
way you can loop through a bunch of plots and datasets and each plot
will be in its own file.

If you use the pdf graphics device then you can produce a single pdf
document with one plot per page.  It may be sufficient to send this to
the client, or you could copy and paste from the pdf or use other
tools to extract the plots or convert to a word document.

Another option is to use the knitr package along with the pandoc
program (or possibly the new Rmarkdown package).  This way you can
create a document with all the plots and convert it directly to a word
document.

The pander package is another option for looping through and sending
plots to a word document.

There is also an R2wd package for writing to word documents, however
one of the possible packages it uses is not free, so be careful of the
usage.

messages.body_plain:
I'll try to pinch hit for Ista since he appears to be busy at the moment. His advice about removing NAs in Vars 4-6 is correct, as usual; here's one way to do it. Call this the split-reshape-combine approach :)

library(reshape2)
library(ggplot2)

# try() is the name of a common function in R, so rename
Try = read.csv(file="Data.csv", header = TRUE, sep = ",")
Try$Date = as.Date(Try$Date, format='%d/%m/%Y')

# Create two sub-data frames: one for the first three variables,
# another for the latter three, both including Date
try0 <- Try[, 1:4]
try1 <- Try[, c(1, 5:7)]

# logical vector to determine if any of Var4-Var6 are nonzero
# in a given row of try1; use this for subsetting below
v <- apply(try1[, -1], 1, function(x) any(!is.na <http://is.na>(x)))

trym0 <- melt(try0, id = "Date")     # 738 x 3
trym1 <- melt(try1[v, ], id = "Date")    # 45 x 3

# Note: variable has different levels in trym0 and trym1

# The two data frames have the same variables, so rbind them
trym <- rbind(trym0, trym1)
# redefine the factor 'variable' to get all of the levels from both
trym$variable <- factor(trym$variable)

# Now plot...
qplot(Date, value, data=trym, colour = variable, size = I(1.2)) + geom_line() +

    facet_grid(variable ~ ., scales = "free")

Observe that you still get a gap in the line plot of Var4, but that's because it has missing values for three years where Vars 5 and 6 do not. The gap is informative. You see the same thing in Var1, but it's less obvious due to the data density. I reduced the point size to reduce overlap of the points - if you like the original point size, just get rid of the argument in qplot(). (size = 1.3 will give you visually larger points).

Dennis

messages.subject: Uneven x-axis spacing for violinplots/boxplots
messages.body_plain:
Is there a way to specify the locations along the x-axis for the violins or boxes for data grouped by a factor? Equivalent to the "at" argument in the standard boxplot function, e.g., if I am plotting 11 groups and I want more space between box 1 and box 2 than between the remaining boxes, I could do

boxplot(x~y, at =c(0, seq(1.5,10.5, by=1)))

How could I do something like this for box plots or violin plots in ggplot2?

Cheers,
Margaret

Dear list members,

I am using geom_bar with position "stack".

How can I include the counts for each section of the stacked bars?

a = c("h","h","h","i","i","i","j","j","j","j")
b = c("n","l","n","l","n","l","z","l","z","z")
data = data.frame(a,b)

d = ggplot(data, aes(a, fill=b))
d + geom_bar(position="stack") +
  coord_flip()

Best,

Manuel

messages.body_plain:
Chang's cookbook, as Doug recommends, is a great resource to keep. In case you don't have access to it, this could get you there.

library(ggplot2)
library(plyr)

a = c("h","h","h","i","i","i","j","j","j","j")
b = c("n","l","n","l","n","l","z","l","z","z")

# data = data.frame(a,b)
#  d = ggplot(data, aes(a, fill=b))
#  d + geom_bar(position="stack") +
#    coord_flip()

bartabledf=as.data.frame(table(a,b))
bartabledf=arrange(bartabledf,a,b)
bartabledf=ddply(bartabledf, "a", transform, label_y=cumsum(Freq)-.1*Freq) # You can mess around with the positioning of the labels in the label_y calculation

ggplot(bartabledf[bartabledf$Freq!=0,], aes(x=a, y=Freq, fill=b)) + geom_bar(stat="identity") +
  geom_text(aes(y=label_y, label=Freq), vjust=1.5, colour="white")+coord_flip()

Best,
Vivek

messages.subject: Re: How to write counts in stacked bars
messages.subject_clean: How to write counts in stacked bars
messages.body_plain:
HI Manuel:

Doug is right about the reference (and it's a good one, BTW), but if
you don't have it, here's one way to produce what you want with
centered labels. Winston's way is a little easier - I tried doing this
without the book.

library(plyr)
library(ggplot2)

a = c("h","h","h","i","i","i","j","j","j","j")
b = c("n","l","n","l","n","l","z","l","z","z")

datos = data.frame(a,b)

# Get the counts
v <- count(datos, vars = c("a", "b"))

# ypos will be the y plotting position of the labels
# in the stacked bar chart, which is why the cumulation
# is necessary
v2 <- ddply(v, "a", mutate, cfrq = cumsum(freq),
                                      ypos = cumsum(cfrq/2))

ggplot(v2, aes(x = a, y = freq, fill = b)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
    geom_text(aes(y = ypos, label = freq)) +
    coord_flip()

Dennis

Thanks!

messages.subject: Aligning error bars with trimmed means
messages.subject_clean: Aligning error bars with trimmed means
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I was interested in looking what a graph with trimmed means looked like in comparison with regular means.

The results are interesting, but the trimmed means are now unaligned with the errorbar geom I also asked for in the code, and it seems a tad bit more complicated to do than the trimmed mean.
I fiddled a bit with the parameters and was able to do something, but I am pretty sure that the trimming proportions are not the same with the mean and errorbars.

I know I should provide some data to illustrate my question, but I do not know how to generate random data.

Here is the function suggested in Wickham's ggplot2 book to get trimmed means :

midm <- function(x) mean(x, trim = 0.5)

It can now replace "mean" in the stat.summary(fun.y = mean, geom = ...) request.
With some trials and errors, I realized I had no idea what proportion  "trim = 0.5" actually meant (i.e., in relationship with "conf.int <http://conf.int> = ..."  of the mean_cl_normal function).

Does 0.5 mean 50% of the data, with 25% on each side?   I noticed that setting trim at 0.05 gave the same graph as with fun.y=mean, but I may be wrong.
I understand that ggplot2 plots means trimmed at 5% by default, am I right?

The errorbar geom is the following:

stat_summary(fun.data= mean_cl_normal, geom="errorbar",

I understand mean_cl_normal is adapted from smean_cl_normal in Hmisc. The confidence interval can be adjusted with conf.int <http://conf.int> = 0.95,  set at .95 by default.

This function produces a vector of summary statistics. I do not know what elements ggplot2 uses in that vector to produce the errorbars.

I created this function believing it would get me closer to what I want:

mean_cl_normalTrim <- function(x) mean_cl_normal(x, conf.int <http://conf.int> = .95)

I figured changing conf.int <http://conf.int> would help, but the combinations I tried (i.e. mean(x, trim=0.1) and mean_cl_normal(x, conf.int <http://conf.int> = .90)) But I do not get  errorbars alligned with the trimmed mean.

Please, can anybody enlighten me?

Thank you,

Pier-Eric Chamberland

messages.subject: Legend position not working
messages.body_plain:
Hello there,

I tried changing the position of the legend in my plot but it doesn't seem to be moving at all and I am not sure what is wrong Everything else in this code works except for the position of the legend. Dear all,

I'm trying to plot humidity in 11 soil levels as a "heatmap". I managed to accomplish this, but my y-axis are in the wrong order. I need to show the top layer at the top ot the graphic, mimicking a cross section of the soil.

Please run this code to reproduce the plot:

---------------------------------------------------------------------
require (RCurl)
require (ggplot2)
require (reshape)
require (scales)

# read data
link <- getURL('http://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/27700634/zday_soil-zwsoi.eq.1.txt')
dry.soil <- read.csv(textConnection(link), header=T, sep='')

# get date from character
tmp1 <- paste(dry.soil$year, dry.soil$month, dry.soil$day, sep='/')
date <- as.Date(tmp1)

# add date amd remove old elements
dry.soil <- cbind(date, dry.soil)

dry.soil <- subset(dry.soil, select = -c(year,month,day,jday))

# constraint date
dry.soil <- subset(dry.soil, as.Date(date) >= '2012-01-01' & as.Date(date) <= '2012-12-31')

# create month factor to produce average
dry.soil$monfac <- droplevels(cut(dry.soil$date, breaks='month'))

#
dry.df <- aggregate(cbind(soil_mois1, soil_mois2, soil_mois3,
                          soil_mois4, soil_mois5, soil_mois6,
                          soil_mois7, soil_mois8, soil_mois9,
                          soil_mois10, soil_mois11) ~ monfac, data=dry.soil, FUN='mean', na.action=na.pass)

# melt data.frame by date
dry.soil.m <- melt(dry.df, id = c('monfac'))
dry.soil.m$monfac <- as.Date(dry.soil.m$monfac)

# plot data
ggplot(dry.soil.m, aes(monfac, variable)) +
geom_tile(aes(fill = value), colour = "white") +
scale_fill_gradient(low = "white",  high = "steelblue") +
scale_x_date(breaks = date_breaks("months"),
             labels = date_format("%b"))
---------------------------------------------------------------------

As you can see, the y-axis is ordered from soil_mois1 to soil_mois11, but I need to reverse it so the top layer is at the top of the graphic.

Any directions?

Thanks in advance,
Thiago Veloso.

messages.subject: Re: Legend position not working
messages.body_plain:
This is not a reproducible example since there is no data to accompany
your code. The following is a minimal toy example to illustrate legend
positioning. Unless you know what you're doing with the
legend.justification() specification, just leave it out. In the
following, the values in legend.position() represent relative x and y
locations in the entire graphics region (not the plot region) where
the legend will be centered.

DF <- data.frame(gp = sample(LETTERS[1:3], 100, replace = TRUE),
                  x = rnorm(100),
                  y = rnorm(100))

ggplot(DF, aes(x, y, color = gp)) +
    theme_bw() +
    geom_point() +
    ggtitle("A title") +
    theme(legend.text=element_text(size=12),
          axis.title.x = element_text(size=17),
          axis.title.y = element_text(size=15),
          plot.title = element_text(lineheight=.8, face="bold", size=17),
          legend.position=c(0.9, 0.9))

The way you defined the legend positioning, it was going outside the
plot region in this example. Play with this by changing the following
in the theme() call above:

(1)  legend.position = c(1, 1)
(2) keep (1) and add legend.justification = c(1, 0)
(3) keep (1) and modify legend.justification = c(0, 0)

That should give you an idea of what legend.justification() does: it
reorients the center of the legend box to the position defined by
legend.justification() relative to legend.position(). The two go
together: legend.position() indicates where the legend box should
originally be centered and legend.justification() repositions the
center relative to legend.position() - its default value is c(0.5,
0.5).

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Aligning error bars with trimmed means
messages.subject_clean: Aligning error bars with trimmed means
messages.body_plain:
See inline.

On Fri, Mar 28, 2014 at 12:03 PM, Pier-Éric Chamberland
<pier.e.ch...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Hi,
>
> I was interested in looking what a graph with trimmed means looked like in
> comparison with regular means.
>
> The results are interesting, but the trimmed means are now unaligned with
> the errorbar geom I also asked for in the code, and it seems a tad bit more
> complicated to do than the trimmed mean.
> I fiddled a bit with the parameters and was able to do something, but I am
> pretty sure that the trimming proportions are not the same with the mean and
> errorbars.
>
> I know I should provide some data to illustrate my question, but I do not
> know how to generate random data.

Really? See Chapter 8 of An Introduction to R and pay attention to the
r<dist>() functions. Other useful functions for creating fake data
include sample() and seq(), among others. A browse through the
archives of this group, StackOverflow or R-help will scare up
literally thousands of examples.

>
>
> Here is the function suggested in Wickham's ggplot2 book to get trimmed
> means :
>
> midm <- function(x) mean(x, trim = 0.5)

That specification sets the *default* trim to 50% on each end - you
can change it in a call, e.g.,

# trim 5% off each end of the data vector x and average
# the remaining elements
midm(x, trim = 0.05)

...but see below.

>
> It can now replace "mean" in the stat.summary(fun.y = mean, geom = ...)
> request.
> With some trials and errors, I realized I had no idea what proportion  "trim
> = 0.5" actually meant (i.e., in relationship with "conf.int <http://conf.int> = ..."  of the
> mean_cl_normal function).
>
> Does 0.5 mean 50% of the data, with 25% on each side?   I noticed that
> setting trim at 0.05 gave the same graph as with fun.y=mean, but I may be
> wrong.
> I understand that ggplot2 plots means trimmed at 5% by default, am I right?

>From the help page of mean (type ?mean at the prompt):

#---------
trim

the fraction (0 to 0.5) of observations to be trimmed from each end of
x before the mean is computed. Values of trim outside that range are
taken as the nearest endpoint.
#--------

Note the **each end** part. If you trim 50% from each end, what are
you left with? Let's find out:

> y <- rnorm(100)
> mean(y, trim = 0.5)
[1] 0.04454727
> mean(y)   # untrimmed mean
[1] 0.02787379
> median(y)
[1] 0.04454727

By generating some pseudo-random data and doing a little snooping, we
discover that the 50% trimmed mean is the median. Change 100 to 101
and you'll get similar agreement for odd numbers of observations.

>
>
> The errorbar geom is the following:
>
> stat_summary(fun.data= mean_cl_normal, geom="errorbar",
>
> I understand mean_cl_normal is adapted from smean_cl_normal in Hmisc. The
> confidence interval can be adjusted with conf.int <http://conf.int> = 0.95,  set at .95 by
> default.

No, it isn't. Since I had to go into the book to check this out, on
p.85 there is a table that says the mean_cl_normal() function defined
in the ggplot2 book is derived from Hmisc::smean.cl.boot(). Did you
check the corresponding help page in Hmisc?

?Hmisc::smean.cl.boot

>
> This function produces a vector of summary statistics. I do not know what
> elements ggplot2 uses in that vector to produce the errorbars.

Again, no - it returns a data frame. See the function's code below.

Also see http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/geom_errorbar.html  to learn
more about what arguments the geom requires.

More generally, bookmark this site, the repository of on-line help
pages for the current version of ggplot2:
http://docs.ggplot2.org/current

>
> I created this function believing it would get me closer to what I want:
>
> mean_cl_normalTrim <- function(x) mean_cl_normal(x, conf.int <http://conf.int> = .95)
>
> I figured changing conf.int <http://conf.int> would help, but the combinations I tried (i.e.
> mean(x, trim=0.1) and mean_cl_normal(x, conf.int <http://conf.int> = .90)) But I do not get
> errorbars alligned with the trimmed mean.
>
>
> Please, can anybody enlighten me?

Evidently you're going through section 5.9 of the ggplot2 book, where
a number of examples are derived to illustrate how one can use
stat_summary() with user-defined functions. For the example you cite,
the code of mean_cl_normal() is elicited by typing the function name
at the prompt:

# library(ggplot2)
> mean_cl_normal
function (x, ...)
{
    try_require("Hmisc")
    result <- safe.call(fun, list(x = x, ...))
    rename(data.frame(t(result)), c(Median = "y", Mean = "y",
        Lower = "ymin", Upper = "ymax"), warn_missing = FALSE)
}

As noted above, it returns a data frame. There is no argument in the
formal argument list that processes a confidence interval
specification; since it does have a ... argument, it won't complain if
you specify conf.int <http://conf.int> = 0.95, but it will silently ignore it.

You should probably look here:

http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/stat_summary.html

In the examples, notice how functions are written to call
stat_summary() - this is so one can supply user-defined variables to
pass to it. More precisely, the fun.y argument of stat_summary() takes
a function with one positional argument and any number of named
arguments with default values. The reason for this is because ggplot2
functions do not pass parameters to functions called within them, so
they need to be specified as default values in the function to be
called. The example on p. 84 of the book is an example of this feature
- to pass the trim = 0.5 argument of mean(), one writes the function
midm() where trim = 0.5 is the default value. Then midm() is passed to
stat_summary() via fun.y.

A caution if you're going through the book: since it was published in
2009, the package has undergone several changes, particularly in the
theming system described in Chapter 8. There are several other places
where the original code may be broken, but I don't have a list
offhand. The two most obvious things that have changed in the theming
system introduced in ggplot2-0.9.2 are:

    * opts() is now theme()
    * theme_*() functions are now element_*() functions; e.g.,
theme_text() -> element_text()

There are several new features that you can find described in the
Themes section of the on-line help pages.

Dennis
